messages.content: I want to design incremental link-time optimization that safely reuses optimized code even when cross-module symbol resolution or optimization dependencies change. It needs to preserve clean-build semantics across weak-symbol replacement, visibility changes, and cross-module function edits. For single-function edits, the target is a median rebuild time of no more than 50% of clean LTO, with no more than a 3% executable runtime regression.

That combines a correctness requirement with two performance limits. Reuse is useful only if the resulting executable still has the semantics a clean build would have with the current inputs. For single-function edits, the median rebuild must take at most half as long as clean LTO, while executable runtime regression must stay at or below 3%.
What does “safely reuses optimized code” mean here? Is unchanged source code enough to justify reuse?

Not by itself. Optimized code can depend on facts learned from another module, including which definition a symbol resolves to or what can be assumed about another function. If one of those facts changes, unchanged source text does not establish that its previously optimized code still reflects a clean build.
So the reference point for correctness is what a clean build would do with the current inputs?

Yes. “Preserve clean-build semantics” makes the current clean build the correctness reference. It does not, by itself, require an identical binary or the same optimization decisions; the point is that incremental reuse must not change the semantics that a clean build would produce.
How does weak-symbol replacement fit into that requirement?

As a general illustration, optimized code might have been produced when a reference resolved to one weak definition. If the definition selected for that reference changes, reusing code that still relies on the former resolution could disagree with a clean build. The requirement is to preserve clean-build semantics through that kind of replacement, not merely to notice that some source file changed.
Is the concern limited to the module containing the weak symbol?

No. The relevant question is whether optimized code depends on the resolution, wherever that code originated. Cross-module optimization makes it possible for a change in one module’s symbol resolution to matter to optimized code associated with another module.
Visibility changes sound different. Why are they called out separately?

Visibility concerns how a symbol may be seen or used across boundaries, so changing it can change assumptions relevant to linking and optimization. The design must preserve clean-build semantics when visibility changes, just as it must when a weak symbol is replaced. Neither case is covered simply by asking whether a particular function’s text changed.
And for a cross-module function edit, could the edit matter to optimized code outside that function?

Yes. In general, an optimization in one part of a program can rely on information about a function in another module. An edit to that function can therefore affect whether the previously optimized code remains appropriate. The requirement covers those cross-module effects while still seeking fast rebuilds for single-function edits.
When you say “optimization dependencies,” do you mean more than ordinary source-file dependencies?

Conceptually, yes. The phrase includes facts an optimization relied on, which need not align neatly with the file that contains the optimized code. The goal identifies changing optimization dependencies as a reason that reuse must be handled safely; it does not prescribe a particular way to represent or manage them.
Then would it be fair to say that an unchanged module is not automatically safe to reuse, but it is not automatically unsafe either?

That is a useful distinction. Whether reuse is safe depends on whether the relevant current symbol resolution and optimization-dependent facts still permit clean-build semantics. The goal is incremental reuse, not a rule that all unchanged code must be reused or that every change forces all optimized code to be regenerated.
I also want to be precise about the rebuild-time number. Does “median rebuild time ≤50% of clean LTO” mean every single-function edit must finish in half the time?

No. The stated measure is the median rebuild time for single-function edits, compared with clean LTO. A median at or below 50% satisfies that time threshold; the wording does not impose a per-edit maximum of 50%.
And the 3% figure is a different kind of limit?

Yes. It limits executable runtime regression, rather than rebuild time. The requirement states a ceiling of 3% but does not specify a workload or a separate runtime-measurement procedure. The time target and runtime limit must both be respected; a faster rebuild is not, on its own, enough.
If reuse made rebuilds much faster but changed the program’s behavior, would being under the 3% runtime limit help?

No. Clean-build semantics are a correctness condition, separate from how long rebuilding or running takes. A program that differs semantically from the current clean build would not satisfy the goal, regardless of its rebuild time or runtime.
Conversely, if behavior is preserved and runtime regression stays within 3%, but the median single-function rebuild takes more than 50% of clean LTO, is the objective met?

Not fully. That would address the stated semantic and runtime conditions, but miss the stated median rebuild-time target. The design goal includes all three: safe reuse, median rebuild time at or below 50% of clean LTO for single-function edits, and executable runtime regression at or below 3%.
Does allowing up to 3% runtime regression weaken the clean-build semantics requirement?

No. Semantic agreement and runtime performance are different properties. The runtime allowance permits a bounded performance difference; it does not permit a different symbol resolution or behavior that conflicts with the current clean build.
I’m trying to avoid treating the three named changes as isolated special cases. Is there a common way to describe what they test?

They each test whether previously optimized code remains valid when information from outside that code changes. Weak-symbol replacement concerns the selected definition; a visibility change concerns how a symbol can be treated across boundaries; and a cross-module function edit can change information used by optimizations elsewhere. In each case, reuse must remain consistent with clean-build semantics.
That does not mean we have already chosen how to detect or respond to those changes, correct?

Correct. The goal and requirements specify what a design must accomplish, not a particular implementation. They do not establish a chosen reuse rule, dependency representation, validation method, or set of measured results.
Could I summarize the central tension as reusing enough optimized code to make a single-function rebuild substantially faster, without letting changed cross-module facts make that reuse stale?

Yes. “Substantially faster” has a precise target here: for single-function edits, the median rebuild time must be no more than 50% of clean LTO. The reuse also has to preserve clean-build semantics despite changing symbol resolution and optimization dependencies, while keeping executable runtime regression at no more than 3%.
One last distinction: are the weak-symbol, visibility, and cross-module-edit cases examples of the correctness requirement, or separate performance targets?

They are explicitly named conditions under which clean-build semantics must be preserved. The numerical performance targets are separate: median rebuild time ≤50% of clean LTO for single-function edits, with ≤3% executable runtime regression. The design has to satisfy those targets without compromising correctness in any of the named cases.

How about caching optimized functions with dependency manifests? Each manifest would track inlined bodies, imported summaries, symbol bindings, and visibility. When something changes, we would rebuild the affected closure.

That is a concrete proposal for deciding when an optimized function can be reused. The cached unit is an optimized function, while its manifest records information from outside that function on which its optimization depends. A change to a recorded dependency would put the function in the affected set rather than letting the cache treat it as unchanged.
Why record an inlined body separately from the function’s own body?

Because an optimized function may contain code derived from another function’s body. An edit to that other function could matter even if the cached function’s own source has not changed. Tracking inlined bodies expresses that dependency directly.
What does an imported summary add? Isn’t the inlined body enough?

An optimization can use information about another function without incorporating its body through inlining. An imported summary represents that kind of cross-module input. Tracking both categories avoids treating every cross-module dependency as though it arose from inlining.
And symbol bindings are there because the same reference might resolve differently?

Yes. If cached optimized code relies on a particular binding, a change in which definition that reference denotes may affect whether the cached code is still suitable. Recording symbol bindings in the manifest connects reuse decisions to the resolution facts used during optimization.
How does visibility belong in that same manifest?

Visibility can affect what an optimization may assume about a symbol across module boundaries. By tracking visibility alongside bindings, the manifest can account for a change in those assumptions even when the symbol’s name and the cached function’s own text remain unchanged.
So the manifest is not just a list of source files that were read?

Right. The proposed manifest describes optimization-relevant dependencies: inlined bodies, imported summaries, symbol bindings, and visibility. Those are more specific than a simple record of which source files exist or which files changed.
I used the phrase “affected closure.” What does that imply beyond rebuilding a directly edited function?

It means considering the effects of a change wherever the tracked dependencies lead, rather than stopping at the first function touched. A function may be affected directly because its own optimization used changed information; other cached functions may in turn depend on information associated with an affected function. The closure is the set reached by following those relevant dependencies, and the proposal is to rebuild that set.
Does this proposal require rebuilding every cached function whenever symbol resolution changes?

No. Its point is to relate a change to the functions whose manifests make that change relevant, then rebuild the affected closure. It also does not claim that every symbol-resolution change is harmless to functions without a recorded dependency; the manifest must adequately reflect the facts that made reuse safe.
Can I say that the cache is keyed only by each function’s source text?

That would miss the proposal’s central distinction. The cached objects are optimized functions, but the manifests also track cross-module inputs to their optimization. Unchanged source text alone would not answer whether a change to an inlined body, imported summary, symbol binding, or visibility affects a cached result.
Suppose a cross-module function edit changes information used elsewhere. Would the affected closure include those other optimized functions?

That is the intended role of the dependency manifests and closure. A cached function that depends on the edited function’s inlined body or an imported summary derived from it would be a candidate for rebuilding. The proposal does not specify a particular representation for those dependencies or a procedure for calculating the closure.
I don’t want to overstate what this establishes. Does describing the cache and manifests prove clean-build semantics are preserved?

No. It proposes a way to make reuse sensitive to the named optimization dependencies and symbol facts. Whether it preserves clean-build semantics depends on whether the manifests capture all relevant dependencies and the affected closure is rebuilt appropriately. No validation result is stated here.
The four manifest categories should stay explicit, then, rather than being collapsed into “things that changed”?

Yes. Inlined bodies, imported summaries, symbol bindings, and visibility identify distinct kinds of information that optimized code may rely on. Keeping them explicit explains why a function can need rebuilding even when its own source is unchanged, and what the proposed cache must account for before reusing it.
And the action is to rebuild the affected closure, not simply discard the entire optimized-function cache?

Exactly. The proposal pairs selective reuse with selective rebuilding: cache optimized functions, use their dependency manifests to identify the affected closure, and rebuild that closure. It leaves the exact mechanics and the resulting performance open rather than asserting that the targets have already been achieved.
Which recorded dependencies would ensure cached functions are invalidated when weak-symbol replacements or visibility changes alter cross-module resolution?

The most directly relevant manifest entries are symbol bindings and visibility. A binding entry would need to reflect the resolution on which the optimized function relied; a visibility entry would need to reflect the visibility assumption it used. The question is whether those recorded facts are sufficient to identify every cached function affected when resolution changes.
For a weak-symbol replacement, is recording that a function mentions the symbol enough?

Merely recording a mention might not express the fact the optimization relied on. The important dependency is on the binding used during optimization: if the selected definition changes, a cached function that relied on the former binding may need to be rebuilt. How to record that binding precisely is still part of the question.
Could visibility change the relevant binding even if the cached function’s own source has not changed?

That is the concern. A visibility change may alter cross-module resolution or an assumption made about it. A function’s unchanged source therefore does not settle whether its cached optimized form remains reusable; the manifest needs to account for the relevant visibility and binding dependencies.
Why track both visibility and symbol bindings rather than treating them as one dependency?

They describe related but distinct facts. A symbol binding concerns which definition a reference resolves to, while visibility concerns how a symbol can be treated across module boundaries. The question is whether recording both lets the design recognize not only a changed binding, but also a changed visibility assumption that affects optimization or resolution.
Do inlined bodies and imported summaries matter to this particular question, or only to function edits?

They could matter if an optimized function used an inlined body or imported summary whose relevance depends on the cross-module resolution at issue. But an inlined-body or summary dependency alone should not be assumed to capture a changed symbol binding or visibility assumption. That is why this question focuses on which recorded dependencies actually trigger invalidation in those cases.
So we need to ask about functions affected indirectly as well as functions that refer to the symbol directly?

Yes. If one cached function depends on information imported from elsewhere, a changed resolution could matter through that dependency even without an obvious reference in its own source. The affected closure in the proposal is meant to capture relevant consequences, but this question asks whether the recorded dependencies are adequate to identify them.
Would it be too strong to say that recording visibility automatically handles every weak-symbol replacement?

Yes. A visibility record and a binding record answer different questions. A weak-symbol replacement can change which definition is selected, so the binding relied on by cached optimized code is especially important. We cannot conclude from the proposal alone that recording visibility, by itself, detects every such change.
Likewise, could recording only the selected definition miss a visibility change that matters even if that definition appears unchanged?

That is a reasonable issue to examine. If an optimization relied on a visibility assumption, the apparent continuity of a binding would not by itself establish that the assumption still holds. The manifest explicitly includes visibility, and the open question is how those entries participate in invalidation when cross-module resolution changes.
What exactly does “invalidated” mean in this discussion? Does it mean the whole cache is thrown away?

Here it means a cached optimized function is not reused without rebuilding when a relevant recorded dependency has changed. It does not imply discarding every cached function. The proposed approach is to rebuild the affected closure while retaining the possibility of reusing functions outside it.
Can we answer the question conclusively just by naming symbol bindings and visibility?

No. Naming them identifies the directly relevant categories, but the word “ensure” asks for more: whether the recorded dependencies accurately cover the resolution and visibility facts each cached function relied on, including dependencies carried through inlined bodies or imported summaries. The proposal names the categories; it does not yet establish that they are recorded or used with sufficient completeness.
Then the core question is whether a weak-symbol replacement or visibility change will reach every cached function whose optimized form relies on the old cross-module resolution?

Exactly. Symbol-binding and visibility records are the direct candidates for detecting that change, and inlined-body and imported-summary dependencies may matter to its propagation. What remains to be determined is whether those records identify the full affected closure so that no function dependent on the altered resolution is reused as though nothing changed.
My hypothesis is that resolver fingerprints covering candidate definitions, prevailing bindings, and visibility will yield zero stale reuses across weak-symbol and visibility mutations.

That proposes a specific answer to the invalidation question: record a fingerprint of the resolution facts relevant to cached optimized code, and use changes in those facts to identify code that should not be reused unchanged. The predicted outcome is zero stale reuses across weak-symbol and visibility mutations. That is a hypothesis, not an established result.
Why include candidate definitions if the fingerprint also covers the prevailing binding?

The prevailing binding describes which definition wins at a particular point. Candidate definitions describe the set from which resolution can select. Including both expresses the hypothesis that tracking only the current winner might not adequately capture changes relevant to future resolution or to assumptions made during optimization. Whether that extra coverage is necessary or sufficient remains to be determined.
What is the role of visibility in that fingerprint?

Visibility is another resolution-relevant fact. A change in visibility can alter what a cross-module reference or optimization may assume, potentially even where the source of a cached function has not changed. Covering visibility makes the hypothesis explicitly address those mutations rather than relying on a binding record alone.
Does “candidate definitions” mean every definition anywhere in the program?

The hypothesis does not specify that scope. It says the fingerprints cover candidate definitions, prevailing bindings, and visibility, but leaves open how the candidates relevant to a particular resolution are identified and represented. That scope matters to assessing the zero-stale-reuse prediction.
And is a resolver fingerprint necessarily just a fingerprint of the prevailing definition’s body?

No. As stated, it covers resolution information: candidate definitions, the prevailing binding, and visibility. Reducing it to the prevailing definition’s body would leave out two of the three named categories and would not express the hypothesis as given.
Suppose a weak-symbol replacement changes which definition prevails. What would the hypothesis predict?

It predicts that the relevant resolver fingerprint would reflect the changed resolution and prevent stale optimized code from being reused. The prediction is specifically zero stale reuses across weak-symbol mutations, including a case where the prevailing binding changes. That still needs to be established rather than assumed from the name of the fingerprint.
What if the candidate definitions change but the prevailing binding stays the same?

The hypothesis deliberately includes candidate definitions as well as the prevailing binding, so such a change is within the information it proposes to cover. It does not say whether every change to the candidates must cause a rebuild, or whether some can be judged irrelevant to a particular cached function. Its outcome claim concerns avoiding stale reuse, not avoiding every unnecessary rebuild.
Would a visibility mutation be captured even if I saw no change in the prevailing binding?

That is one reason visibility is named separately. Under the hypothesis, a relevant visibility change would be visible in the resolver fingerprint rather than disappearing because the prevailing binding appears unchanged. Whether the resulting invalidation reaches every affected cached function is part of what the zero-stale-reuse prediction puts at issue.
Is “zero stale reuses” a claim that no optimized function is ever reused after one of these mutations?

No. It means no cached optimized function is reused when the changed resolution or visibility makes that cached form stale. Reuse of unaffected functions is compatible with the hypothesis; indiscriminately rejecting all reuse is not what the wording asserts.
How does that connect to the dependency manifests we discussed?

The manifests are the proposed place to track what cached functions depend on. Resolver fingerprints are a hypothesized way of covering the resolution-related facts—candidate definitions, prevailing bindings, and visibility—so changes to those facts can matter to reuse decisions. That connection describes the idea; it does not establish that the coverage is complete.
Are inlined bodies and imported summaries replaced by these fingerprints?

The hypothesis does not say so. It focuses on avoiding stale reuse across weak-symbol and visibility mutations by covering resolver facts. Inlined bodies and imported summaries remain distinct categories of optimization dependency in the caching proposal; nothing here concludes that resolver fingerprints subsume them.
Does the prediction cover every type of cross-module function edit too?

Not as stated. Its zero-stale-reuse prediction is expressly about weak-symbol and visibility mutations. A cross-module function edit may involve other optimization dependencies, so extending the prediction to every such edit would go beyond this hypothesis.
Could the fingerprints change more often than strictly necessary without contradicting the hypothesis?

Yes. An overly broad fingerprint could lead to rebuilding code that was actually safe to reuse, while still avoiding stale reuse. The stated prediction is about zero stale reuses across the named mutations; it does not assert minimal invalidation or a particular rebuild-time result.
So even if the zero-stale-reuse prediction held, would that alone establish the median rebuild-time and runtime targets?

No. Avoiding stale reuse addresses a correctness risk. The broader goal separately calls for median rebuild time for single-function edits of no more than 50% of clean LTO and executable runtime regression of no more than 3%. This hypothesis makes no claim that those numerical targets have been met.
What is the precise uncertainty I should keep attached to this idea?

Whether fingerprints covering candidate definitions, prevailing bindings, and visibility actually identify every cached function made stale by weak-symbol or visibility mutations. The proposed coverage is meant to yield zero stale reuses in those cases, but the outcome has not been demonstrated in the information given.

I want to implement resolver fingerprints and dependency-closure invalidation, then test weak-symbol and visibility mutations and cross-module edits against clean builds, rebuild-time budgets, and runtime budgets.

That sets out both the implementation work and how to assess it. Resolver fingerprints would address changes in cross-module resolution, while dependency-closure invalidation would determine which cached optimized functions need rebuilding. The tests would compare results with clean builds for semantics and check the stated rebuild-time and executable-runtime limits. This is a plan, not a report of completed tests.
Can you separate the two implementation pieces? I don’t want “fingerprint” and “closure” to sound interchangeable.

They have different roles. A resolver fingerprint represents resolution-related facts whose changes may matter to cached optimized code. Dependency-closure invalidation uses recorded dependencies to identify the functions affected by a change, including effects that extend beyond the immediately changed function. A fingerprint can indicate that a relevant fact changed; the closure determines the scope of rebuilding.
The resolver facts we have in mind are candidate definitions, prevailing bindings, and visibility, correct?

Yes—that identifies the resolver-fingerprint approach being implemented. Those are distinct aspects of cross-module resolution. Including them in the implementation plan does not yet establish that the resulting invalidation will catch every stale reuse; that is among the things the tests need to examine.
And the dependency closure still matters for an edit to a function in another module?

Yes. A cross-module function edit may affect optimized functions that depend on information from the edited function. The planned closure invalidation is meant to rebuild affected cached functions rather than consider only the edited function. Testing cross-module edits against clean builds checks whether that treatment preserves the required semantics.
What should “against clean builds” mean in this plan?

For correctness, the current clean build is the semantic reference. After each tested weak-symbol mutation, visibility mutation, or cross-module edit, the incremental result needs to preserve the semantics of a clean build with those current inputs. The plan does not require claiming that the executable files are identical.
Does checking the clean-build result also tell us whether the rebuild-time budget was met?

No. Semantic comparison and rebuild-time measurement answer different questions. The time target is a median rebuild time of no more than 50% of clean LTO for single-function edits. Comparing semantics with a clean build would not, by itself, establish that time comparison.
What about the runtime budget? I mean the runtime of the executable, not how long the rebuild takes.

Right. The executable runtime regression limit is no more than 3%, separate from the rebuild-time target. The plan calls for checking that limit as well as clean-build semantics and rebuild time. It does not state a measured regression or specify a runtime workload.
If a tested weak-symbol mutation changes resolution, what is the plan trying to find out?

It is trying to find out whether the implemented resolver fingerprints and invalidation prevent reuse of optimized code that depends on the changed resolution, so the incremental result retains clean-build semantics. The testing also belongs alongside the rebuild and runtime budget checks; detecting the change correctly would not alone establish those performance targets.
Would the visibility tests ask a similar question even when a function’s source is unchanged?

Yes. A visibility mutation can alter cross-module resolution or optimization assumptions without editing the cached function’s own source. Testing that case against a clean build examines whether the implementation invalidates affected cached code rather than reusing it solely because its source was unchanged.
I want the cross-module edit tests included explicitly, not folded into weak-symbol or visibility tests.

They are explicitly part of the plan. Weak-symbol mutations, visibility mutations, and cross-module edits are all to be tested. A cross-module function edit can exercise dependencies on information from another function even when the issue is not a change to symbol resolution or visibility.
Does this plan say we should rebuild everything whenever any of those cases occurs?

No. Dependency-closure invalidation is a selective approach: rebuild the functions identified as affected by the relevant change. The planned tests need to assess correctness and performance, but the plan does not prescribe rebuilding the entire optimized-function cache for every mutation.
Nor should we assume that selective invalidation already gives the speed target, right?

Correct. Selectivity is the proposed means, not a measured result. The median single-function rebuild-time target remains ≤50% of clean LTO, and the tests against rebuild budgets are intended to determine whether the implementation meets it.
What if a rebuild is fast and the executable runs within the 3% limit, but the incremental output disagrees semantically with a clean build?

It would fail the clean-build semantics requirement. The performance budgets do not excuse stale reuse across weak-symbol replacement, visibility changes, or cross-module function edits. The plan therefore checks semantic agreement separately from the two performance limits.
And what if clean-build semantics are preserved but one of the performance limits is missed?

Then the correctness part would be addressed for the tested case, but the full goal would not be established by that result. For single-function edits, the median rebuild-time limit is ≤50% of clean LTO, and the executable runtime regression limit is ≤3%; the plan is to check those budgets, not to infer them from correctness.
So what can I accurately say has been decided at this point?

The plan is to implement resolver fingerprints and dependency-closure invalidation, and to test weak-symbol and visibility mutations and cross-module edits against clean-build semantics, rebuild-time budgets, and executable-runtime budgets. It does not yet report whether invalidation is complete, whether any stale reuse occurs, or whether the numerical budgets are met.
Run the ResolverFlip-200 weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases. For each case, compare prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes with deterministic clean LTO.

That gives ResolverFlip-200 two explicit comparisons against a deterministic clean-LTO reference: which bindings prevail, and what hashes the optimized functions have. The weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases exercise the resolution changes at issue. The activity is specified, but no comparison results are stated yet.
Why compare prevailing bindings separately from optimized-function hashes?

They answer different questions. Prevailing bindings show which definitions resolution selected. Optimized-function hashes show whether the optimized functions being compared match at the hashed level. Checking both helps distinguish a resolution difference from a difference visible in the optimized code, without assuming that one comparison substitutes for the other.
If the bindings agree with deterministic clean LTO, have we shown that cached optimized functions were safe to reuse?

Not solely from binding agreement. A cached function can depend on optimization information beyond the identity of the prevailing binding. That is why the activity also compares optimized-function hashes. Neither comparison should be described as a reported outcome before the cases are run and examined.
And if an optimized-function hash agrees, does that establish that the prevailing binding was correct?

No. Hash agreement concerns the optimized function being hashed; it does not replace a direct check of prevailing bindings. The activity explicitly calls for both comparisons against deterministic clean LTO.
What does the deterministic part of the clean-LTO comparison contribute?

It makes the clean-LTO reference suitable for a meaningful hash comparison: repeated reference builds should not differ merely because their output is nondeterministic. The activity names deterministic clean LTO as the comparison point; it does not report any particular match or mismatch.
Should I describe ResolverFlip-200 as 200 successful cases?

No. ResolverFlip-200 is the named activity here. Its name alone does not report how many cases passed—or that any have passed. The stated work is to run its weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases and make the specified comparisons.
What are we looking for in a weak-replacement case?

Compare the prevailing binding after the weak replacement with the binding from deterministic clean LTO for the same case. Also compare the optimized-function hashes with that clean-LTO reference. Those observations bear on whether code was reused despite a resolution change that mattered; the activity does not supply the observations themselves.
Is the visibility-flip comparison different?

It uses the same two stated comparison categories: prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes against deterministic clean LTO. The change being exercised is visibility rather than weak replacement. Keeping the cases distinct lets the activity examine both kinds of resolution mutation without assuming they affect cached functions in identical ways.
Suppose a hash differed from the clean-LTO hash. Can we immediately label that a stale reuse?

A differing hash identifies a difference to examine; the activity alone does not establish its cause. In particular, the wording does not state that every hash difference is stale reuse or that hash equality is the entire clean-build semantics criterion. The comparison is evidence to inspect, not a result or diagnosis supplied in advance.
Could I say this run will prove the zero-stale-reuse hypothesis for all possible symbol changes?

That would overstate its scope. ResolverFlip-200 covers the named weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases and compares them with deterministic clean LTO. Those comparisons can evaluate the prediction for the cases exercised, but the activity does not claim results or extend its coverage to every possible symbol change.
Does this activity also measure median rebuild time as a percentage of clean LTO?

Not as stated. Its specified measurements are prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes. The broader rebuild-time target is a median of no more than 50% of clean LTO for single-function edits, but this activity does not say to measure rebuild times or report that target.
What about executable runtime regression?

That is also outside the comparisons named for this activity. The broader limit is no more than a 3% executable runtime regression, but ResolverFlip-200, as described here, compares prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes; it does not report runtime measurements.
I want to be clear that deterministic clean LTO is the baseline for both checks, not just for the hashes.

Yes. The instruction is to compare both prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes with deterministic clean LTO. A binding comparison against a different reference would not express the stated activity.
So for now, the accurate description is the run and its comparison points, without a pass count or a conclusion about stale reuse?

Exactly. Run the ResolverFlip-200 weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases, and compare prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes with deterministic clean LTO. No pass count, observed discrepancy, or conclusion about stale reuse is provided.
ResolverFlip-200 matched clean-LTO prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes in all 200 cases, with zero stale cache reuses.

For the 200 ResolverFlip-200 cases, both comparisons matched the clean-LTO reference: the prevailing bindings and the optimized-function hashes. The observed stale cache reuse count was zero. Those are results for the cases exercised, not a claim about every possible change.
Do “all 200 cases” and “zero stale cache reuses” describe the same observation?

They are related but distinct. “All 200 cases” gives the scope over which the clean-LTO binding and hash comparisons matched. “Zero stale cache reuses” states the observed reuse outcome over those cases. Keeping both makes the result more precise than reporting only that the comparisons matched.
Can I say that no prevailing binding differed from clean LTO in ResolverFlip-200?
Yes. Matching clean-LTO prevailing bindings in all 200 cases means no binding mismatch was reported in that set. The optimized-function hashes also matched clean LTO in every one of those cases.
Does the hash result cover just a few selected cases?

No. The result states that optimized-function hashes matched clean LTO in all 200 cases, alongside the prevailing-binding matches. It does not give a separate subset or a different count for the hash comparison.
How should I connect this to the weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases we ran?

ResolverFlip-200 exercised weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases. Across its 200 cases, the prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes matched clean LTO, and there were zero stale cache reuses. The result does not break the 200 cases down by mutation type, so it is best not to invent separate counts for the two categories.
Does this mean the cached optimized functions were identical to clean LTO in every conceivable respect?

The reported comparison is of optimized-function hashes, together with prevailing bindings. Those matched in all 200 cases. The result does not separately report a byte-for-byte comparison of entire executables or every other property one might compare.
Could I describe the reference as deterministic clean LTO?

Yes. Deterministic clean LTO was the reference specified for the ResolverFlip-200 comparisons. The reported result is that its prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes matched the ResolverFlip-200 results in all 200 cases.
What does the zero-stale-reuse observation say about resolution changes in these cases?

It says that none of the 200 exercised cases produced an observed reuse of cached optimized code that had become stale. Together with the matching prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes, that gives a concrete result for the weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases in ResolverFlip-200. It should remain scoped to those cases.
Earlier I predicted zero stale reuses across weak-symbol and visibility mutations. Can I report the observation without claiming more than was measured?

Yes: ResolverFlip-200 observed zero stale cache reuses in all 200 of its weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases, with clean-LTO matches for prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes. That states the observation directly without extending it to mutations outside the cases exercised.
Would “the fingerprints can never miss a visibility change” be an accurate conclusion from this?

No. The evidence reports what happened in ResolverFlip-200: all 200 comparisons matched and zero stale cache reuses were observed. It does not make a universal claim about every possible visibility change or every possible way resolution could vary.
Is there any reported mismatch to investigate within those 200 cases?
None is reported for the two specified comparisons. Prevailing bindings and optimized-function hashes matched clean LTO in all 200 cases, and the stale cache reuse count was zero.
Does this result also cover cross-module function edits?

The reported ResolverFlip-200 result concerns its weak-replacement and visibility-flip cases. It does not state an outcome for cross-module function edits, even though those edits are part of the broader incremental-LTO goal.
And have we learned anything here about the median single-function rebuild time?

No rebuild-time measurement is included in this result. In particular, the all-200-case matches and zero stale reuses do not establish whether median rebuild time for single-function edits is ≤50% of clean LTO.
What about the ≤3% executable runtime regression limit?

Yes. The full proposal has to be read together: use changed answers to decide invalidation for tracked summary queries, but invalidate conservatively when a read is untracked. Otherwise ‘only on changed answers’ would incorrectly make an unknown answer look safe.

For the recorded query, the partition has a known answer to compare with the current one. The matching answers do not override the resolver check. The proposal retains that check as a separate condition before reuse. The answer-based rule narrows when tracked summary information calls for invalidation; it does not make resolution changes harmless.

Under the proposed rule, the changed answer triggers invalidation of the partition that depended on it. Passing resolver checks addresses a different class of dependency and does not make the old summary answer valid again.
